1:
Nobody reads the prohibition as absolute; the disagreement is how to limit it. Jerome puts the difficulty in a sentence: how then could Paul judge the offender at Corinth, or Peter convict Ananias? Chrysostom answers that what is forbidden is bitterness, not correction: the sinner is still to be set right, as a physician applies a remedy and not as an enemy taking revenge, and the prohibition falls on men loaded with great evils who arraign others for small ones. Augustine draws the line at evidence rather than office: where an act cannot be innocent we may judge, but where it might be done from either mind the duty is to put the better construction on it, rashness being worst when we cannot see the intention. Gill, Barnes and Henry exempt the magistrate and the Church court and leave only the private censure that reads words and deeds at their worst; Barnes adds that we cannot help forming opinions of evil conduct, so what is condemned is the haste and the refusal to allow anything that might excuse. Calvin treats it as medicine for a common disease, noting how strangely enjoyable the inspection of other men's faults is.

Two witnesses stand apart. Pseudo-Chrysostom will not allow even the well-meant correction the others save, and asks whether a man who merely refrains from judging has earned forgiveness, since nobody is pardoned an old sin by declining a new one. Hilary takes the saying to be about judging God rather than one's neighbour: human verdicts rest on uncertainties, and to pronounce on the divine promises from what is doubtful is a case where the sin lies not in judging wrongly but in judging at all.

The measure is agreed to be a current proverb. Lightfoot gives the rabbinic form, that in the measure a man metes it is measured to him, and Gill says the same; Barnes adds that it holds both of how men will treat us and of the rule God will use. Clarke reads it as plain consequence, the severity we dealt out returning as the severity we suffer. Ellicott states it exactly: an unjust judgement of ours does not bring down an unjust judgement from God, but the harshness we measured out becomes, by a retributive law, the measure of what is justly dealt to us. Wesley calls the words awful, a man in effect choosing whether God shall be severe or merciful to him.

On the mote the interest is lexical and proverbial. Clarke prefers splinter, which bears an analogy to a beam where mote does not; Robertson agrees it is dried wood rather than dust and makes the beam a joist sticking out grotesquely; Ellicott notes that satirists everywhere have made the point, the Gracchi complaining of sedition and Clodius of adultery. Chrysostom illustrates it with men who denounce a monk for one good meal while drinking to excess themselves. Barnes keeps the disproportion simple, small offences in others against large ones at home. The fathers vary the application: Jerome aims it at those in mortal sin who will not forgive a trifle; Pseudo-Chrysostom at teachers, for whom the same act is a beam where a layman's is a mote; Hilary again goes his own way and makes the beam the sin against the Holy Spirit. Calvin names both faults, the sharp sight that comes of having no charity and the indulgence that shelters our own. On the remedy there is no dispute. Gill, Clarke and Wesley hear the word hypocrite aimed at a reformer who needs reforming, Ellicott adding that such hypocrisy is worse for not knowing itself; and Barnes and Robertson agree the beam comes out so the eye may work, the verb changing from gazing at a thing to seeing through it, the point being never to abandon the brother but to become fit to help.
6:
The allegory is read two ways, and the difference matters. Augustine defines the terms: the holy thing is whatever it would be impiety to corrupt, the pearls are spiritual things too precious to be despised, and the two animals answer to two faults, dogs assaulting the truth and tearing it, swine merely despising it and treading it down. Barnes finds that distribution set out as an introverted parallelism, the first clause answering to the fourth and the second to the third, so that the dogs rend and the swine trample and the verse must be read across itself rather than straight through. Clarke reaches the same result by transposing the members outright, and Wesley notes the same transposition, the latter of the two things proposed being treated first. Against them Ellicott assigns the figures the other way, making the dogs the type of impurity and the swine of ferocity, and suggesting that the swine's rage is the disappointment of having taken pearls for grain.

On what the holy thing is, the grammatical readers agree against the allegorists. Ellicott, Clarke and Robertson take it for flesh that had been offered in sacrifice, which no unclean person and no unclean beast might eat; the objection is not that the dogs would refuse it, but that giving it to them would profane it. Gill traces the same law, that torn flesh was ordered to be given to dogs while nothing consecrated ever was. Barnes alone resists, taking the holy thing for anything connected with religion and the pearls for the doctrines of the gospel.

Pseudo-Chrysostom presses the sacramental application hardest. The holy thing is baptism and the grace of Christ's body; the pearls are the mysteries of truth, lodged in the deep meaning of Scripture as pearls lie shut in shells in the deeps. He divides the animals by the marks of uncleanness in the law, the dog unclean in every respect and the swine in one only, and reads the first as the Gentiles and the second as heretics, who at least call upon the Lord's name. But he will not carry it through: the benediction is in fact given to Christians who live as brutes, not because they deserve it, but lest, being more grievously offended, they perish outright.

Calvin narrows the precept further, and against a use he thinks it has been tortured into. Ministers cannot tell the children of God from the rest, so the doctrine of salvation is to be held out to all without distinction, and charity forbids pronouncing anyone desperate at first sight; the dogs and swine are only those who by clear evidence have shown a hardened contempt, so that the disease appears incurable. He too separates the pair, giving brutal stupidity to the one and rage to the other, and names the two classes he has met: those who turn free justification and election into an encouragement to sloth, and those who assail the doctrine and its ministers with reproaches. Wesley makes it practical, warning against talk of perfection to men wallowing in sin and against declaring one's own experience to persecutors, while insisting that reproof itself is nowhere forbidden.

Augustine adds the caution the precept needs: to hide a truth is not to utter a falsehood, and the Lord who never spoke falsely still had many things to say that His hearers were not able to bear. That some who heard Him rejected what He said does not make His teaching a casting of pearls, since He gave to those able to receive. Chrysostom says why the caution is needed at all: such men feign meekness in order to learn, and attack once they have learned. Rabanus and the Gloss leave the door ajar, the dogs having returned to their vomit while the swine only wallow, and the words lest perchance allowing that they may yet wisely turn.
7:
The joint is disputed. Jerome reads the turn as positive instruction: having forbidden prayer for the things of the flesh, He now shows what we ought to ask. Augustine hears an objection instead: why forbid me the giving of holy things, when I cannot see that I have any holy thing at all? Pseudo-Chrysostom offers a harder connection, that the precepts already given lie beyond the reach of human virtue, so that He sends men to God, with whose grace nothing is impossible.

Whether the three verbs differ is a second question. Augustine unfolds them carefully, asking for soundness of soul to do what is commanded, seeking for the discovery of truth, knocking for entry into possession, then allows it were better to refer all three to instant prayer. Pseudo-Chrysostom makes them three kinds of labour, prayer, study and good works, since a man at a door not only cries out but strikes with his hand. Chrysostom takes the added words as demands for vehemence, the seeker casting all else from his mind. Henry agrees that seeking and knocking mean more than asking: we must second our prayers with our endeavours or we tempt God.

On the limit of the promise there is no dissent. Augustine grants that a man asking in faith for the necessities of this life is heard mercifully and also not heard mercifully, the physician knowing better than the sick man what the sickness needs; God often withholds what we would have to give what we should rather prefer, and delay is recommendation rather than refusal. Calvin turns this into a rule, that our affections being blind we are not competent judges and must restrain the heart from asking anything not agreeable to God's will. Henry puts it in the nursery, where the child may ask for a sharp knife to play with, and denials in love are better than grants in anger. Calvin then guards the whole from being read as cause and effect: God keeps watch over sleeping believers and anticipates their wishes, and faith itself goes before all prayer in order and in time, we are bidden to pray that faith may be exercised, not that God may be roused.

The phrase being evil divides the readers. Chrysostom denies that the race is called evil at all: paternal love is named evil only by comparison with a goodness it cannot approach. Jerome takes it at full weight, the Apostles condemned in their persons along with a race whose heart is set on evil from infancy; Gill presses harder still. Clarke calls the depravity radical and diabolical, then turns the verse against a doctrine, asking whether such a Father could reprobate to unconditional damnation any creature he has made. Ellicott holds the balance: the words admit the fact of depravity and in the same breath deny that it is total, the natural affection left in us being what makes human fatherhood a fit parable of God's.

The images are read at two levels. Gill notes that a serpent is not unlike a fish, an eel especially, and that bread and fish were common food in a fishing country; Ellicott finds the homeliness worth remarking, addressed to the peasants of Galilee; Robertson observes that some stones look like loaves, as the tempter knew. Lightfoot and Clarke both recall the proverb Seneca preserved for a grudging benefit, stony bread. Remigius and Rabanus allegorise, loaf and fish becoming doctrine and baptism for the one, charity and faith for the other, set against ignorance, unbelief, hatred, treachery and a despair that stings backward like a scorpion. On the good things all converge: Remigius, Calvin, Clarke and Ellicott take the promised gift to be chiefly the Holy Spirit, in whose grace every other good thing comes. Wesley closes the doctrinal part of the sermon with the condition attached, that we imitate the God of love.
12:
Everything turns on whether the connective carries weight. Chrysostom insists it does: the saying is not all things whatsoever, simply, but all things therefore, as though besides what has just been asked of God something must also be done by us; and the standard set is not what we would have God do for us, which invites the plea that we cannot, but what we would have a fellow-servant do. Calvin denies the whole procedure. The particle is superfluous, glued to proverbs by long use, and since Matthew is gathering detached sayings rather than reporting one discourse, the sentence must be read by itself. Ellicott finds a third route, by way of likeness rather than exchange: man's highest blessedness is to be like the God who gives good things to those who ask. Pseudo-Chrysostom hears only the thread of the opening precept resumed, and Augustine makes the link blunter, that we can hardly press a request on God while refusing the equal who presses one on us.

All the careful readers limit the rule, on three different grounds. Augustine works from the words: some Latin copies add good things, an insertion he takes to forestall the man who would have a crime committed for his advantage, though he judges it unnecessary, since will properly belongs only to the good and in the wicked is better called desire. Ellicott limits it by the state of the one obeying: the rule is safe only when our own will has been purified, reciprocity in folly or in lust being altogether alien from the mind of Christ. Clarke limits it by office, quoting Selden's prisoner who asks the judge whether he would be content to hang in his place: neither acts as a private man, both having consented beforehand to the law.

That the maxim was already current nobody disputes. Lightfoot tells the story, the Gentile asking to learn the whole law standing on one foot, beaten with a staff by the first rabbi and made a proselyte by the second, who gave the rule in its negative form. Ellicott adds the reply attributed to Aristotle when asked how we should treat our friends. Robertson lists the negative form in Tobit, Philo and Confucius, and marks the difference: Jesus puts it positively. Clarke draws the opposite temper from the same evidence: God seems to have written it on the hearts of all men.

On the closing clause there is agreement with one reservation. Cyprian sums the whole body of commands in this one; Gill calls the verse the epilogue of the discourse; Henry allows that it is nowhere found in the older books in so many words, yet is the concurring language of them all, and turns it round: by this rule the law of Christ is commended and the lives of Christians condemned. Calvin confines the claim to the second table. Augustine notices the reservation himself, that here it is not called the whole Law, as elsewhere, so that room is left for the command about loving God; then he closes the gap, since whoever loves his neighbour must love love itself, and God is love.

Henry puts obedience in three steps: do what we ourselves acknowledge fit and reasonable, reckon others as much entitled to justice as we are, and suppose ourselves placed in their case, no strained supposition, since we do not know how soon their case may be ours. Barnes calls the rule the balance-wheel of the moral world, correcting irregularity of movement as a governor does in an engine. Gregory raises the standard higher, to returning good for evil and better for good. Calvin sees why it is so seldom kept: every man is a subtle doctor of justice where his own advantage is concerned, and justice would prevail if we were as good scholars in practising charity as we are instructors in preaching it.
13:
What the strait gate is nobody agrees. Gill makes it Christ himself, the door into the church below and the holiest above, and adds that faith is not the gate but the grace by which a man enters it. Wesley makes it the holiness described in the foregoing chapters, and nothing else. Clarke makes it the rule just given, doing to every man as you would be done by, the only gate he thinks the words can allude to, though he will not quarrel with those who read it as repentance. Ellicott takes way and gate together as the way of obedience, allows the deeper sense in which Christ calls himself the way and the door, then cautions that this does not make union with Him a substitute for holiness, only the means of it. Pseudo-Chrysostom sets the two gates against each other as persons, Devil and Christ, explaining the epithets by character rather than power: the one broad by the license of unbridled pride, the other strait by humility, since He whom the world cannot contain shut himself within a virgin's womb.

On the picture there is more agreement. Lightfoot finds behind it the rule of the Jewish lawyers, a private way four cubits broad and a public way sixteen; Clarke repeats the measurements. Barnes thinks of the walled city with its great thronged avenues and its private gates that few are seen entering. Ellicott suspects a town actually in sight, its narrow pathway leading to the needle's eye of a gate. Robertson presses harder, the way not merely narrow but compressed, like a defile between high rocks, and remarks that the broad road is in every town, with glaring lights that lure to destruction. Barnes and Robertson both separate strait from straight, the second meaning not crooked and the first pent up, a confusion the older rendering has fostered. Clarke prefers a different reading altogether, on the authority of most of the best copies: not because the gate is strait, but how strait it is.

Jerome hears an exactness in the verbs that the others pass over: of the broad way it is said that many walk, of the narrow that few find. The broad needs no search and is not found at all but presents itself; and many who do find the narrow way desert midway, caught by the pleasures of the world. Chrysostom reads the fewness as a warning against measuring by numbers, the many being merely sluggish. Calvin turns it on the reader: a small company makes men careless, and we think it strange to be forcibly separated from the vast majority, as though we were no part of the human race; men ruin one another by example, and each rushes on because, being ruined in a crowd, he does not believe he is ruined. Wesley puts it shortest: nobody need look for the wide gate, men come to it of course. Clarke counts the losses in stages, few finding the way, fewer abiding, fewer still walking in it, fewest of all persevering, and insists that nothing makes the way narrow except sin.

Chrysostom alone faces the obvious objection, that the same Lord calls his yoke easy and his burden light. His answer is that calling the way strait is what makes it light, since it sets men watching and stirs desire, as a combatant takes heart on seeing the prince admire the struggle. The way is strait, he adds, but not the city, so we look for no rest here and expect no sorrow there. Calvin says the same more soberly: the bitterness is soothed by a joyful recompense. Ellicott, weighing the word destruction, argues that it means waste and the loss of all that makes existence precious rather than extinction, and will not shut out deliverance altogether, since the lost sheep was found and the perishing son came home.
15:
Who the false prophets are is contested, two readers of the same name contradicting each other. Pseudo-Chrysostom argues the warning is aimed at heretics and nobody else: not at Gentile or Jewish teachers, since heretics come under the Christian name, and not at Catholic teachers who are merely sinners, for such have no purpose to destroy. Chrysostom decides the opposite way: the aim is less at the heretic than at the man whose life is corrupt behind a face of virtue, since among heretics a good life may often be found and among these never. The later readers each name their own quarry: Gill the Scribes and Pharisees with their free will and traditions of the elders; Clarke the man who enters the ministry for a living and clothes himself with the fleece; Wesley whoever describes a broad way to heaven; Robertson the Judaizers and Gnostics, with the remark that wolves are more dangerous than dogs and hogs.

Henry divides the danger in two, false commission and false doctrine, the first to be feared even where the teaching is true. Lightfoot takes the clothing literally, not woollen cloth but sheepskins. Gregory puts the sharpest test: in quiet times the hypocrite keeps the skin on; a persecution strips it off him.

What the fruits are is the real dispute, and Ellicott states it as a dispute. Those who weigh the ethical side of religion find them in the outcome of doctrine in life and deeds; those who dread heresy find them in doctrines, since good works may themselves be the clothing that hides the wolf. Ellicott decides for the first, since Scripture calls good works the fruits of faith. Gill holds the second, because a false teacher may so behave as never to be discovered by his conduct, so that his doctrines and their effects are the only test. Augustine stands between: almsgiving and prayer displayed before men are the clothing and not the fruit; but he adds a test the others lack, that when temptation withdraws whatever the display was aimed at, it soon appears which animal is underneath.

The two trees were long ago pressed into service for two natures. Augustine answers that it is not said a good tree cannot become bad, but that it cannot bear evil fruit; the tree is the soul, the fruit the works, so a man who would do good must first become good, as snow may cease to be snow but can never be warm. Jerome puts the objection from cases, asking how Moses sinned at the water of contradiction, how Peter denied his Lord, and how an unbelieving father-in-law gave good counsel. Gill insists on the order: the tree is good before the fruit, and the fruit only shows it so. Clarke turns the words against those who hold that great crimes may consist with a state of salvation, or that the righteous necessarily sin in their best works. Wesley enters the most careful qualification in the chapter: the goodness spoken of belongs to the doctrine rather than the character, a bad man preaching this doctrine being sometimes the instrument of converting sinners; he does not claim that all who speak truth are true prophets, only that none are who do not.

On the fire, Ellicott and Henry both note the words are the Baptist's, repeated unaltered; Henry draws a moral, that novelty of expression is no virtue. Chrysostom finds two punishments, to be cut down and to be burned, and says ten thousand hells would be lighter than the loss of that glory and being held in hate by Christ. Cyril of Jerusalem addresses the hypocrite in the room, who came to spy out what is given rather than receive it, and tells him the Judge is inexorable. Wesley asks the question that stings the pulpit: how dreadful is the teacher who has brought no sinners to God.
21:
Jerome sees the two halves of one warning: above, men with the robe of a good life were refused for their impious doctrine; here fellowship is forbidden with those sound in doctrine who destroy it by their works. Augustine raises the harder difficulty, that the Apostle says no man can call Jesus Lord but by the Holy Ghost, while these evidently do and are shut out. His answer is that the Apostle means by the word the speaker's will and understanding, a man properly saying a thing only when his voice expresses his purpose, whereas here it is used of one who neither wishes nor understands what he says. Chrysostom asks why the Father's will is named rather than the Son's, and answers that it was fitted to their weakness, the will of the Son being no other; the Judge reveals himself at the sermon's close. Ellicott makes that the marvel of the passage: at the outset of his ministry he claims with entire calm to be the one before whom all will give account.

Whether the works pleaded were real was disputed in Chrysostom's day; he reports two answers before his own. Some held the plea is a lie and that this is why they are lost; he objects that no one would dare lie to the Judge in his presence. Others held the sins came later; he objects that this destroys the very thing the passage is meant to prove, that neither faith nor wonders avail where the life is bad. His own answer is that grace has often worked through unworthy men for others' sake, since not all are fit for all things: some of pure life with little faith, others the reverse, God using each to draw on the other.

Henry and Barnes bring forward the men who prophesied without being sent, and the traitor who cast out devils; Barnes argues that God may give the power of raising the dead to a wicked man as readily as the skill of healing to a wicked physician. Wesley draws the blunt conclusion: the working of miracles is no proof a man has saving faith. Gregory turns it into a rule, the Church despising heretics' miracles because they carry no mark of holiness, the proof of which is not wonder-working but loving our neighbour and thinking better of him than of ourselves. Hilary alone shifts the weight to the human side: something must be put forth out of ourselves, that we may will the good, rather than boast of what He enables.

On the words I never knew you the commentators divide along their own lines. Barnes makes the verse decisive: Christ does not say he once knew them and then rejected them, or that they were pardoned and fell away, but that he never knew them, which he calls the most decided proof that believers do not fall from grace. Calvin reads it the same way, the Lord knowing who are his, the clause keeping weak minds from being shaken when men of great reputation desert. Clarke and Wesley render the phrase identically, that he never approved of them: men who saved many souls were themselves never saved. Jerome catches the tense: it is those who work iniquity, not those who have worked it, so repentance is not shut off, the sentence falling on men who keep the desire of sinning when opportunity is gone.

The application is left to the pastors. Clarke asks how many are finger-posts on the road to eternal life, pointing out a way they do not walk. Henry warns the respectable that men may go to hell by the gates of heaven, secret haunts of sin under a visible profession ruining the hypocrite. Pseudo-Chrysostom sees the scene: each man's work speaks while his mouth is silent, and to call once is not enough for a man in terror.
24:
Chrysostom states the occasion: some would admire the sayings without adding the showing forth that lies in action, and are warned beforehand. Robertson adds that hearing sermons is dangerous business if they are not put into practice. The backward reference raises a question that has run through the chapter. Ellicott takes these sayings of mine as evidence that the discourse is continuous and not a compilation of fragments, and Augustine had said the words show the sermon complete in the precepts by which the Christian life is formed. Calvin, who has twice insisted that Matthew gathered detached sayings, concedes only that the relative covers not one class of sayings but the whole amount of doctrine.

Pseudo-Chrysostom builds the boldest reading on a point of wording: the hearer is not accounted wise but likened to a wise man, and the wise man is Christ, who built his house, the Church, upon the rock of faith, the foolish man being the Devil, whose house is the ungodly built on the sand of unbelief. Every element then works twice over: the rain is doctrine, falling from clouds raised either by the Spirit or by the spirit of the Devil; the winds are the spirits of the virtues or else unclean spirits; the floods are the evangelists, or else men overflowing with many words, out of whose belly come rivers of dead water. Against the Devil's house the rain of true doctrine descends and that house falls, which is the Gentile world with its idols broken down. He adds a distinction the others do not make: the great ruin is the failure of the foundation itself, not fornication or homicide, from which a man may rise again by penitence.

What the three assaults signify divides everyone. Hilary reads a progression: the showers are the allurements of smooth and gently invading pleasures with which faith is first watered as by spreading rills, then the torrents of fiercer desire, then the whole force of the tempest. Augustine assigns rain to the darkness of superstition, winds to the rumours of men, floods to the lust of the flesh. Gill has four rather than three, temptation, persecution, the stream of a man's own corruption, and the wind of strange doctrine. Clarke also makes three kinds of trial: providence, the passions of men, and Satan. Ellicott declines the whole exercise: the wind and rain and floods hardly admit of individual interpretation except by an unreal minuteness, and stand collectively for the violence of persecution and temptation from without.

On the rock there is more convergence than the allegories suggest. Ellicott makes it primarily repentance and obedience, the assent of will and affections and not of the lips, then allows two deeper senses, the disciple who was named Rock and Christ himself as the rock beneath it. Calvin puts the test where it belongs: true piety cannot be told from its counterfeit until the trial comes, and all build on sand who do not dig deep enough to deny themselves. Jerome fixes on the material: sand cannot be bound into one mass, and on it all heretical teaching is built so as to fall.

The picture was drawn from life. Barnes and Ellicott both describe the torrent-bed, dry for months and suddenly swollen; Ellicott adds the stranger tempted by the ready-made level surface, who would become a by-word among people who knew the ground. Clarke quotes two rabbinic parables of the same shape, the tree with many branches and few roots against its opposite, and the house with stones at the foundation against the house with brick there, then judges that the dignity the figure gained in passing through these hands is sought in vain in the older version. Barnes ends where the parable does, with the man who perhaps laid for others the foundation on which they build for heaven, and laid none for himself.
28:
What the wonder was worth divides the readers; Chrysostom and his namesake part company again. Pseudo-Chrysostom takes it coldly: a satisfied mind brings forth praise, an overcome mind wonder, and we admire only what we cannot praise worthily, so that their admiration went to Christ's glory and not to their faith, since men who believed would not have wondered. He notes too that it was the common people and not the chief among them, and that had such men been present the silence would have been broken by contradiction, for where there is more knowledge there is stronger malice. Chrysostom reads the same verb warmly: the multitude, being of benevolent temper, is easily persuaded by truth, and so far from being repelled by the loftiness of the injunctions they would not leave him, but followed him down the mountain. Rabanus offers both readings, the wonder being either the astonishment of those who did not believe or the reverence of all for so great wisdom. Hilary compresses it to a line: they measured the efficacy of his power by the might of his words.

Augustine turns to who was listening, the wording suggesting a crowd beyond the disciples. Either this sermon was for the disciples only and the discourse on the plain was another occasion, or one sermon was spoken to apostles and multitude together and set down by two evangelists in different words with the same substance. He then does something more ambitious, referring every precept of the sermon back to the seven beatitudes with which it opened, pairing the contemptuous word with poverty of spirit, the rebellion of carnal delight with mourning, the love of enemies with mercy, and singleness of intention with purity of heart.

On what the authority consisted in there is no disagreement. Chrysostom and Jerome both fix on the formula: he spoke with reference to no one else, as Moses and the prophets had, but prefaced each law with but I say unto you, adding what the Law seemed to omit and altering what he chose, as the Lord of Moses himself. Gill says it lay less in the matter or manner than in the method, truths delivered in his own name by one speaking as a lawgiver. Wesley calls it a dignity peculiar to him as the great Lawgiver.

The contrast with the scribes is documented rather than asserted. Lightfoot supplies the decisive instance: no scribe's sermon carried weight without the formula that the rabbins have a tradition, and even the greatest of them was not received, though he discoursed all day, until he said he had heard it from his own teachers. Ellicott observes that what astonishes is less the I say unto you than the entire absence of any teacher's name, the scribe leaning on precedent as a lawyer leans on his cases; here it is the prophet, or rather the king, who speaks. Robertson says the scribes feared to express an idea without propping it on a predecessor, and dismisses the preserved specimens as the dullest collection of disjointed comments. Barnes and Clarke charge them with triviality and the splitting of controversial hairs, and Clarke reports that many manuscripts and nearly all the old versions add the Pharisees here.

The chapter closes on a chorus of verdicts. Clarke calls it the most strict, pure and sublime sermon ever delivered to man, and yet so simple that almost a child may apprehend it. Barnes holds that in no language is there a discourse to compare with it, and were there no other evidence of a divine mission this would serve. JFB will not gloss it at all, saying such teaching is best left in its own transparent clearness. Robertson alone keeps the ending in view: the discourse finished with a house falling on the sand like the crash of a great tree, and nothing was done to smooth the outcome.
